408.t: Free and Easy: the 1959 Quincy Jones Europe tour
408.s: The show fails, the band stays in Europe, Quincy runs short of money, and they open for Basie at the Olympia.
408.ch: Studio years and the 1959 Europe tour
408.q: Yeah. And um so I was getting a little bored, I mean. And you must remember that in 1959 I went to Europe with the Quincy Jones band. There was a show called “Free and Easy.” We were in costume, it was a remake of St. Louis Woman, sound, uh songs by uh Harold Arlen, score by Quincy Jones and Billy…

408.t: Quincy keeping the band together in Europe
408.s: After the show folded, Quincy booked the band himself, shared his last francs and rented an Orient Express car.
408.q: When the story is told that’s why Quincy is who he is. I mean why doesn’t he do more for jazz — man, I remember we did a tour of Yugoslavia, one of the toughest tours I’ve ever been on in my life, this same period. In other words, the show closed, I think the show lasted four or five months and it…

860.t: Return to England, Denmark, and the Barber-Sunshine band
860.s: After the immigration matter was sorted out, he started with Chris Barber and Monty Sunshine in 1953, rehearsed in Copenhagen, then broke away after about a year to form his present band, whose members he lists.
860.ch: Later band, return visits and marching band
860.q: i know dick knows this but this is all for historical records so we might as well get it done oh that was only technical really that got sorted out when i got home that's when we i started with chris barbara and mommy sunshine that was in what yeah that was 1953 right we went to denmark first…

801.t: Simon's missed chance with Noble Sissle
801.s: Lawrence got the best breaks; Simon could have gone overseas with Noble Sissle swapping with a French bassist.
801.q: Simon could have went off with Noble Sicilis. They wanted to swap places, my brother. Noble Sicilis bass player was a pure Frenchman.

910.t: Back to Washington, Charlie Byrd trio and Woody Herman tour of 1959
910.s: He left Dinah for family life in 1956, hooked up with Charlie Byrd at Washington clubs, and toured England and Saudi Arabia with Woody Herman in 1959.
910.q: Yeah. When I left Dinah, because my wife and I had a son and I said well I’ve got to try domesticated life. And so I went to Washington in October of ‘56 and I started working at a club that had just opened up in January and they had a house trio and they were bringing in names on the weekends.…

328.t: Woody Herman's band and staying in Europe
328.s: Joining Woody Herman, a downbeat mix-up story, then an offer of concerts on the continent led to eight years in Europe.
328.q: It was spontaneous. It wasn’t planned. Impromptu. I was playing with Woody Herman. And at that time when you joined a band you didn’t have any rehearsals or anything like that. You joined the band and you went right on the concert stage and played right there and you had to sight read everything…

514.t: Sitting in with Lionel Hampton and touring Argentina and Europe
514.s: He sat in at the Metropole Lounge, was hired on the spot, flew to Buenos Aires, stayed a year, grew tired of few solos, and toured Europe jamming in hot clubs.
514.q: Very interesting. What happened, I got to New York and as I was telling a couple of students today, they wanted to know how did I motivate myself and get ahead. I said go to all the jam sessions. Even if it’s not a jam session, if you go to hear somebody play and you feel you’re sure you can play,…

353.t: Touring with Dick Hart, Basie and Ronnie Scott's
353.s: Her first road work with Dick Hart, the 1968 European tour with Basie, and Ronnie Scott's, where she had to join the British musicians' union.
353.q: Well the only time that I really traveled with the band was much later, in the late 60s, when I went to Europe with Basie. And let me see it was after Joe Williams had left and they needed somebody, they needed somebody that could sing the blues, and I mostly sang rather than playing, those guys…

698.t: Free and Easy European tour with Quincy Jones
698.s: The Free and Easy show failed in Paris, and the 19-piece band barnstormed Europe for ten months; Budd Johnson was the only one to chase down.
698.q: Quincy Jones. That was the show called “Free and Easy.” I think it was in 1959, 60. And we went over there with the show, which failed in Paris, and that picture, well that’s not the way we were sitting in the show, but that picture is the background, it’s what the show was built on. We only had…

994.t: Travelling with the pans and the lost instrument in Latvia
994.s: He must travel with his own pans because each is handmade; British Airways lost his instrument in Latvia and the band played without him.
994.q: Yeah. Oh I have stuff like that for sure. Or there’s stuff that like I used to be able to play that like now it’s like I don’t even want to play that anymore because it’s so hard, but then other people can play it, because it’s written down and they wanted the technical challenge to do that. You…

551.t: Choosing songs with Basie and singing in other languages
551.s: Basie chose only Alright O.K. You Win; Williams then sings a line of Smack Dab in the Middle in German and talks about travel.
551.q: Yeah. You don’t forget the languages. I’ve traveled over there so much.

470.t: Joining Quincy Jones's European band tour
470.s: On George Russell's recommendation Baker joined Quincy Jones's band after two rehearsals in a section with Melba Liston and Curtis Fuller, and was listed on a bootleg as 'plus one other trombone'.
470.ch: Teaching programs, mentors, White House and other bands
470.q: Anthony Ortega. We called him Batman. So it meant I made a lot of very valuable connections that I would then really be able to capitalize on down the road, because we all were very good friends. So that was good. Then, I hadn’t spoken much about Quincy [Jones]. Quincy called when they needed…

108.s: Berlin welcome, trains, a yodeling bus driver in Switzerland, and the Basie repertoire.
108.q: In Europe, it was my first time. We went to – I think we went first to Germany, in Berlin. I remember. I had just studied a little German. The burgmeister, the mayor of the town, came and welcomed us: “Willkommen Sie, Graf Basie zu Berlin” or something. Count, of course, didn’t understand what he –…

686.t: Length of the tour, Europe and management control
686.s: The stint lasted about two months with a month in Europe; management kept the band on edge, as in the missing passport of Rudy Johnson.
686.q: We started. Hit New Orleans, New York. Then we went to Europe for probably a month, which was great. It was my first time in Europe.

66.t: The Woody Herman band, walking out, and the offer to go to Europe
66.s: Glaser replaced her sidemen without warning with a Woody Herman group. She walked out, then Gale's office called with the English ban offer.
66.ch: 52nd Street, Birdland and the bop musicians
66.q: : Ok yes. You know what really happened when I was on this engagement. My brother always comes around. He could really play drums but he never worked at it, piano - Jerry Burley, my brother. He's a dancer. He used to tap dance like Baby Laurence, the greatest dancer in the world, just never worked…

427.t: Kansas City, St. Louis, the Bay Area, England and the Apollo
427.s: A run of dates in Kansas City, Topeka, St. Louis, Oakland for Slim Jenkins, back to Texas, then England with Frankie Newton.
427.q: And then, I left and went back to Kansas City to play some dates there at a hotel there called the Theresa Hotel. So I played there a coupla weeks. Then I went to Topeka, Kansas...played up there for a coupla weeks...came back to Kansas City...hung around there for a coupla weeks, just havin'…

81.t: Jazz Train: bad management, Europe and Johnson's wish to revive it
81.s: Harper says four shows with Johnson lacked good management; Jazz Train in Britain and Ireland drew ten-minute finales, and Johnson wants it back.
81.ch: Herbie Harper and Rasch's notes on Johnson
81.q: The unfortunate part about the whole thing was that -- of the shows I worked with J. C. on -- and we did four -- we never had good management. They were either racketeers in the legitimate sense or underworld, because both
